beats: Hook (her puzzle): a qubit is either |0> or |1>: one look tells you which. Now it is either |0> or |+>, and you may look once. Why can't you always tell? (line_qc_arrow_one_look: the friend slides a box with one peephole across the table; two blank answer cards for the code to letter). Cast as in QC04-01: the tinkerer and the friend.

Complex numbers (12:23-16:39): a + bi; the conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part; a ket is a column vector, a bra its conjugate row (dagger = transpose, then conjugate every entry) (line_qc_arrow_dagger_mirror: the mirror lays the column of two tiles down as a row).

Why amplitudes, not plain probabilities (her clip 17:09-17:42, "interference is driven by complex numbers"): amplitudes carry a sign or a phase, so they can cancel as well as add, like ripples in a tank (line_qc_arrow_ripple_tank). Honest wording: negative amplitudes already cancel; why nature uses complex ones is Scott Aaronson's blog post (title and year in FACTS.md); never say probabilities interfere. Skip the student question 18:07-18:37.

A qubit is a unit arrow: |0> = (1, 0), |1> = (0, 1), any state alpha|0> + beta|1> (22:19-24:57); the X basis |+> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2, |-> = (|0>-|1>)/sqrt2. A real qubit with exactly this geometry: a photon's polarization, vertical = |0>, horizontal = |1>, diagonal = |+>; a filter passes or blocks one photon (line_qc_arrow_filter_bench). kit2d draws the arrows and axes; the drawings never do.

Superposition is relative to a basis (her clip 24:57-25:48): |+> is a mix of |0> and |1> but a plain basis state in the X basis, like a diagonal avenue that is a zigzag in grid steps and one straight street on its own (line_qc_arrow_grid_walk).

Inner product = overlap: how much of one arrow lies along the other, its shadow (line_qc_arrow_stick_shadow); orthogonal (no shadow) means perfectly distinguishable in one look (|0> vs |1>); any overlap means they can be confused: <0|+> = 1/sqrt2 (26:55-31:33, her clip 29:56-30:55). Skip the student question 28:43-29:04.

The hook answered: measured in the Z basis, |0> always gives 0, |+> gives 0 or 1 half the time each, so one 0 cannot tell them apart, like a coin with a sun on both faces vs. a fair sun-and-moon coin after one toss (line_qc_arrow_two_coins). Caveat on screen: the coins copy only the statistics of one chosen question; |+> is not secretly 0 or 1, and asked in the X basis it answers + every time.

One look vs. many copies (Q24-08 70:00-72:49): with many copies the statistics give it away (line_qc_arrow_coin_piles: two equal piles); with one copy no single look is always right (the best single try, about 85%, only if FACTS.md keeps it).

Length 1 because the probabilities |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 add to 1 (33:42-34:52), and in the X basis |alpha+beta|^2/2 + |alpha-beta|^2/2 adds to 1 too (35:20-38:21): one jug of water, split differently by each pair of glasses, never more or less than one jug (line_qc_arrow_jug_glasses). Close on her clip 25:48-26:16: practise until it is like 8 + 3 in your head (reuse line_tally_pages).
Cover (line_qc_cover_04_02; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the tinkerer holds up a big round frame with one arrow pointing between its two guide marks; the friend tilts his head.
